segments.text: And let's talk about the two other figures, which we'll return to time and time again.
Ulysses S. Grant and Robert E. Lee.
So who was Grant?
So this is a man who failed at farming, failed at business, failed at his role in the peacetime army.
Then when the war came, the war revealed the genius.
So he'd known a lot of failure.
He'd known a lot of setbacks.
And his wartime record shows that he learned to deal with those things.
He had a great, tremendous relationship with his wife, a very strong family life, a family he loved.
I think that was the rock for him.
But during the war, what he exhibited was an absolute willingness to break rules, to take risks,
to take responsibility for what he was doing, whether it was a success or a failure,
and not to be cast down by things that didn't work.
If something didn't work, he'd say, OK, that didn't work.
this.
He very famously, when he got to Virginia in 1864 and took over the army to Potomac, he had
all these subordinates who were saying, well, what if General Lee does this?
What if General Lee does
that?
He finally said, why don't we start not worrying about what General Lee is going to do
and let General Lee worry about what we're going to do.
I mean, he just had, he was unflappable,
under stress.
He was the perfect person to end up heading the Union armies.
And he and Lincoln,
that, and he proved indispensable.
But he has this reputation as a butcher, Grant the Butcher.
That's something that former Confederates and some Democrats in the North fastened on him.
His preferred way of fighting wasn't just kind of slug it out.
It's really interesting to compare
his record in the war and Lee's record in the war before they wound up opposing each other in
Virginia in a really bloody Overland campaign.
Grant's total casualties in all his great battles
they met were 37,000.
Lee's were over 98,000 in the same period.
The bloodiest general in U.S.
history by far in terms of how many of his men get shot is Robert E. Lee.
The most careful
demographic study of any Civil War army is one done of Lee's army by a scholar named Joe Glattar,
and Joe figured out that if you were a soldier in Robert E. Lee's army, you had a 73% chance of
becoming a casualty.
Grant's casualties get high when he runs into Robert E. Lee,
just like everybody else.
So the butcher tag is completely unfair about Grant.
He's also known as
a drunk.
And people have gone back and forth on that, whether he just had a weakness, couldn't
hold his alcohol very well, or was okay as long as his wife was around and he had a key staff
officer to help him.
The point is, alcohol never got in the way of anything Grant did during the
war.
And he had a superlative record of delivering victories when the United States needed them,
and Lincoln figured that out.
And the absolute proof of his stature because of this is that in
March of 1864, Congress decided to dust off the rank of three-star general, lieutenant general,
and give it to Grant.
The only person who ever had that rank was George Washington.
The man, Jorge.
I mean, he is the man.
And so they're saying, okay, Grant, you get the rank the man had.
And that shows there's never been anyone else who got it.
You're the first.
And then he would also be the first to get a four-star rank in the United States Army.
There couldn't be a better indication of his stature than he got Washington's rank.
Winfield Scott had had it by brevet.
Grant got the actual rank.
So, in part, the Grant the Butcher label was from the Overland Campaign that we'll talk about.
It is from the Overland Campaign.
Because the military decisions made there, many would argue that those are critically important for the success of the war.
Yes.
He and Lee are often compared, but for the last year of the war, they're operating on, it's not apples to apples,
because Grant is general-in-chief and is managing the entire war effort.
He's managing what Sherman's doing and what Sheridan's doing and what Nathaniel Banks—
Lee is an army commander.
He can recommend things to Jefferson Davis, but he never commands more than an army.
And so he never operates at the level that Grant did.
Very late in the war, he was made general-in-chief when it was so late that it didn't matter.
So who was Robert E. Lee?
In April 1861, Lee was offered command of the Union Army.
He was.
and chose Virginia instead.
He did.
What was he actually choosing in that decision?
Was he choosing home?
Was he choosing honor?
Was he choosing slavery?
And maybe just zooming out,
what do we need to understand in the early steps about Robert E. Lee?
Who was the man?
Well, Lee is sort of the antithesis of Grant in some ways.
Lee is from an aristocratic family.
Grant was from a solidly middle-class family.
Lee's from an aristocratic family at the very top of the Virginia aristocracy.
He has uncles who were prominent to sign the Declaration of Independence.
His father was a famous commander under George Washington.
His father's the one who said that Washington was first in war, first in peace, first in the hearts of his countrymen.
That's Lee's father, who was later a prominent Virginia politician.
Lee's idol is George Washington.
He patterns himself on Washington.
He differs from him in some ways, but he patterns himself on Washington.
He considered Washington the most admirable person in United States history.
And then, of course, he almost undoes the work that George Washington put in place during the American Revolution.
He chose Virginia.
He didn't leave.
He didn't resign his commission in the United States Army to go with the Confederacy.
He resigned his commission in the United States Army to go to Virginia, which wasn't in the Confederacy yet, become the head of state forces in Virginia.
But then when Virginia went into the Confederacy, he took his Confederate commission and ended up as the third-ranking officer in Confederate service.
And he makes an easy transition to a Confederate loyalty.
I think it's his loyalty to Virginia and what that means.
That means his family.
And, of course, that means slavery.
That's part of what that loyalty is.
He's devoted to the slaveholding South as well as to Virginia.
Virginia is a subset of that.
That is in one bundle with Lee.
It's all, but he also had been an ardent U.S.
nationalist
earlier in his career and a very successful military officer.
Winfield Scott thought he was the greatest soldier in the Army,
and Scott, he probably really thought except for me.
But Scott is a great soldier that people don't remember that way
because he became a kind of job of the hut figure by the time of the Civil War.
He's enormous, weighs 350 pounds, has to be winched onto his horse.
But he was a very smart guy, and he thought very highly of Lee.
Lee was a superb soldier, as he would show during the war.
But he's on the wrong side.
Maybe just to throw in a few more characters,
I do think the folks on both sides that are of the more radical persuasion are quite interesting.
Somebody you spoke about, I'm not sure where,
I think it might have been in your lecture series about Thaddeus Stevens.
Thaddeus Stevens.
Thaddeus Stevens is one of the most radical of the radical Republicans.
He's a congressman from Pennsylvania who people think people say harsh things now in Congress.
Thaddeus Stevens just eviscerated people.
And he was way out.
I mean, he was an ardent abolitionist and for equal rights for women in many ways.
And he picked up a number of courses and championed them.
I think in your lecture, you mentioned this thing, which I just love this slime line.
This is his kind of line.
He's sitting in the House of Representatives, and one of his opponents, and he's speaking.
And one of his opponents starts to come down to the floor, and he says, and this is a paraphrase,
I'm going to pause while my colleague from wherever he was from slinks across the floor of this house
and adheres to his seat by his own slime.
That's a great line.
Impromptu.
Women used to ask for locks of hair from famous people.
and he was completely bald and wore a full wig.
He had a woman stop him on the steps of the Capitol Way
and ask for a lock of his hair,
took his whole wig off and said,
Madam, have them all.
No, it's very good.
But of the radical persuasion.
Oh, absolutely.
Yes, he defined it.
He is the character in Birth of a Nation
that Stoneman, the character in Stoneman,
the evil radical Republican named Stoneman
is patterned on, that is.
